title: The Imitation, again
tomorrow: can a nun's tiny chores really count for something big?

cards: Ten at night, the kitchen. A college form on the table, a pen nobody is holding. A dad says Oregon is too far.
A daughter says he never wanted her to go anywhere. Both are partly right, and both are getting louder. Somebody shuts a cabinet harder than the cabinet deserved.
Then one of them goes quiet. Not to win. Just to breathe.
And the next sentence comes out different. A small old book, The Imitation of Christ, bets everything on that pause, and it has an order for nights like this one.

teach.b: The Imitation, the book tradition credits to Thomas à Kempis, gives the order in book two, chapter three: first keep yourself in peace, and then you'll be able to bring peace to others.
Back on the climb, we met that chapter's two people, the peaceable one and the heated one. Today, a different door into the same line. Look at where Catholics meet peace at Mass.
Just before communion, the priest prays with Jesus's words from John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, do I give unto you."
Then comes the sign of peace: a handshake, a nod, a hug for whoever is next to you. Notice the order.
The peace is given first, then passed on. Nobody in the pew has to manufacture it on the spot. That's the Imitation's point too.
Peace first doesn't mean faking calm, or winning by going silent. It means getting your own heart back before you try to fix anyone else's.
The book is blunt about why: a troubled person, it says, turns even good things toward harm and suspects everyone.

teach.h: YOU CAN'T HAND WHAT YOU DON'T HOLD.
teach.b: You can't hand across the table what you aren't holding.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the sign of peace isn't small talk. It's a gift handed down the pew, and the Imitation is a manual for holding on to it long enough to pass it along.

how: Catholics share a sign of peace at Mass just before communion, after the priest prays with Jesus's words from John 14:27; many keep The Imitation of Christ as a book to read a few lines at a time.

o: a small old book on following Christ, inward first
a Church rulebook for behaving well at Mass
a medieval guide to copying saints' daily habits

games.q: where the peace comes from — tap the pairs.

s: peace first means staying quiet so the other person wins
the Imitation means getting your own heart back first, not losing on purpose.
at Mass, Jesus's words about peace come just before communion
the priest prays with them, and then the sign of peace is shared.
the Imitation says to calm others down first, then yourself
the order runs the other way: peace in you, then peace for others.

games.q: two teammates are fighting in the group chat, and both want you on their side, right now. what does the Imitation's order point to first?
o: pick whoever is more right, fast, so it ends.
settle yourself first, then answer without adding heat.
mute the chat until they sort it out alone.
games.why: the Imitation's order: keep yourself in peace first, and then you can bring peace to others. muting dodges it; a fast verdict adds heat.

practice: Unclench, in order: jaw, shoulders, hands. Let your hands rest open in your lap, ready to receive something. Bring to mind the one argument you're carrying today, and keep your hands open while you hold it.
If you pray, you can ask for his peace first, before any words.

wordCard.voice: The Imitation. A small book on following Christ, with an order of operations: peace in you, then peace for others.

orig.note: Latin: peace. the older Latin Mass greets the people with pax Domini, the peace of the Lord, before communion.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: peace first, because whatever needs fixing can wait for one slow breath. Talk tomorrow.
